posts.headline: The ADEA applies to employers with at least how many employees?
posts.explain: The ADEA protects workers age 40 and older, with no upper age limit. 15 is the Title VII number, the classic mix-up.

SHRM-CP & SCP Question of the Day: The Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) applies to employers with at least how many employees?
A. 15
B. 20
C. 50

posts.alt_a: Answer: B. 20 employees. The ADEA protects workers age 40 and older, with no upper age limit. 15 is the Title VII number, the classic mix-up.

youtube_quiz.question: The Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) applies to employers with at least how many employees?
youtube_quiz.explanation: The ADEA covers employers with 20+ employees and protects workers 40 and older. 15 is the Title VII threshold.

posts.headline: A new hire starts on Monday. When is Section 2 of Form I-9 due?
posts.explain: Section 2 is due within 3 business days of the first day of work, so a Monday start means Thursday. Section 1 is due day one.
posts.sourceLine: Source: 8 CFR 274a.2(b)(1)(ii); USCIS Handbook for Employers (M-274), 4.0

posts.facebook_first_comment:
✅ Answer: C. Thursday.
The employer has 3 business days after the first day of work to complete Section 2, so a Monday start is due Thursday. (Section 1 is due on day one. If the job lasts less than 3 days, Section 2 is due on day one too.)
📚 More practice: https://shrm.thegreygym.com
posts.alt_q:
SHRM-CP & SCP Question of the Day: A new hire starts work on Monday. When is Section 2 of Form I-9 due?
A. Monday (day one)
B. Wednesday
C. Thursday
D. The following Monday
posts.alt_a: Answer: C. Thursday. Section 2 is due within 3 business days of the first day of work, so a Monday start means Thursday. Section 1 is due day one.

youtube_quiz.question: A new hire starts work on Monday. When is Section 2 of Form I-9 due?
youtube_quiz.explanation: Section 2 must be completed within 3 business days of the employee's first day of work. Monday start = due Thursday. Section 1 is due day one.

posts.headline: Under the FLSA, how long must employers keep payroll records?
posts.explain: Payroll records, union contracts and sales records: 3 years. Time cards and wage-rate tables: 2 years. Mixing up the two is the trap.
posts.sourceLine: Source: 29 CFR 516.5 and 516.6; U.S. DOL WHD Fact Sheet #21

posts.facebook_first_comment:
✅ Answer: C. 3 years.
Payroll records must be kept for at least 3 years. Supporting records like time cards and wage-rate tables need 2 years, which is why B catches so many people.
📚 More practice: https://shrm.thegreygym.com
posts.alt_q:
SHRM-CP & SCP Question of the Day: Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), how long must employers keep payroll records?
A. 1 year
B. 2 years
C. 3 years
D. 7 years
posts.alt_a: Answer: C. 3 years. Payroll records, union contracts and sales records: 3 years. Time cards and wage-rate tables: 2 years. Mixing up the two is the trap.

youtube_quiz.question: Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), how long must employers keep payroll records?
youtube_quiz.explanation: FLSA: payroll records 3 years (29 CFR 516.5). Supporting records such as time cards and wage-rate tables: 2 years (29 CFR 516.6).
